HCM is the most common inherited cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. It is characterised by a dominant mutation in sarcomeric proteins, and can present with asymptomatic hypertrophy or symptomatic hypertrophy with outflow tract obstruction. Histological evaluation reveals myocyte disarray. HCM can also present with non-obstructive hypertrophy with high-risk features such as left atrial enlargement, ventricular remodelling, fibrosis, and arrhythmias. Dilated cardiomyopathy is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in middle-aged athletes. It is characterised by a dominant mutation in sarcomeric proteins, and can present with asymptomatic dilation or symptomatic dilation with heart failure. Histological evaluation reveals wavy myocytes. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is the most common inherited cause of sudden cardiac death in older athletes. It is characterised by a dominant mutation in interstitial collagen, and can present with asymptomatic thickening or symptomatic thickening with heart failure. Histological evaluation reveals amyloid deposits.

Edward's Syndrome is also known as Trisomy 18. The clinical features of this condition include prominent calcaneus, microcephaly, clenched hands with index and fifth finger index over the third finger, severe developmental delay, and structural heart defects. Infants with this condition often have low birth weight, underdeveloped jaw, and small tongue. Most infants with this condition do not survive past the first year of life.  Apert's Syndrome: This is a genetic disorder that affects the development of the skull and face. People with this condition have an abnormally shaped head, closely set eyes, and fused or deviated septum. Apert's syndrome is caused by a mutation in the FGFR2 gene.  Down's Syndrome: This is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. People with Down's syndrome have characteristic facial features, including a small mouth, small ears, and a low-set nose. Other features include upslanting eyes, a large tongue, and a single transverse palmar crease.  Klinefelter's Syndrome: This is caused by an extra X chromosome. Men may be infertile, tall, and have less muscle mass.  Patau's Syndrome: This is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 13. People with this condition have characteristic facial features, including a small mouth, small tongue, and smooth epicanthic folds. Other features include developmental delay, seizures, and structural heart defects.

Cushing’s disease is a form of hypercortisolemia caused by a pituitary-secreted ACTH that causes excessive cortisol production. A - CORRECT. This means that less cortisol is produced and so the hypercortisolemia is exacerbated.B - INCORRECT. Glucocorticoid receptor antagonists are not as effective as glucocorticoids at providing negative feedback on the hypothalamus, so less CRH and ACTH would be released, resulting in less cortisol being produced.C - INCORRECT. This is describing Addison’s disease.D - INCORRECT. Radiation therapy to treat a pituitary adenoma would remove or damage the pituitary gland, meaning less ACTH would be released. This would result in less cortisol being produced and so the hypercortisolemia would be relieved.

Sentinel cells are a type of cell that act as the first line of defence against infection. They are cells that are constantly monitoring the environment for signs of infection, and if detected, they will activate an inflammatory response.  They are all nucleated cells, and can be found in different tissues.  The main sentinel cells are:• Macrophages• Mast cells• Dendritic cells• Microglial cells• Langerhans cells Natural killer cells are not sentinel cells, as they do not act as the first line of defence. They are instead part of the second, more direct, line of defence. NK cells are important in the direct killing of target cells that have been infected by a virus.

HCN4 channels are hyperpolarised cyclic gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels. Activation of beta adrenergic receptors via noradrenaline causes an increase in cAMP production which in turn activates HCN4 channels. This causes an increase in the 'funny current' and therefore an increase in pacemaker slope and an increase in heart rate (positive chronotropy). Ryanodine receptors are the receptors on the SR which are activated by increased intracellular Ca2+ to cause further release of Ca2+ from the SR. This has a number of effects on the cardiac cycle. The increased Ca2+ will have a positive inotropic effect (increase force of contraction) and also cause the SR to clear faster, meaning the muscle relaxes faster (positive lucitropy).

Monoamine oxidase inhibitors prevent the breakdown of tyramine, which is found in foods such as cheese. This leads to an excess of tyramine which causes the build up of noradrenaline and adrenaline. This causes a hypertensive crisis.  They do not prevent the breakdown of tryptophan, so tryptophan does not build up. However, the build up of serotonin does. This is why MAOIs are contraindicated in those who have suffered a first degree or higher reaction to e.g. Ibo.  Alcohol is a CNS depressant and so while it may affect performance, it is unlikely to be a contraindication.

Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT I) is an enzyme found on the outer mitochondrial membrane. It catalyses the reaction of an Acyl-CoA molecule with carnitine, to form Acylcarnitine. Acylcarnitine can then be transported across the mitochondrial membrane via the carrier acylcarnitine-translocase. Once on the inner mitochondrial membrane, CAT II catalyses the reaction of Acylcarnitine with CoA, to regenerate Acyl-CoA and carnitine. Acyl-CoA is now available for beta-oxidation.  CAT I and CAT II are both mitochondrial enzymes, but CAT I is found on the outer membrane and CAT II on the inner.

Haloperidol and chlorpromazine are both conventional anti-psychotics. They can cause extrapyramidal side effects such as dystonia, akathisia and parkinsonism (which explains the symptoms the patient was initially suffering from). However they can also cause life-threatening ADRs such as madleir's disease. Clozapine overcomes this problem and is therefore used when other drugs are ineffective. However it has its own serious ADRs which is why blood monitoring is required.  Fluoxetine is an SSRI and benzodiazepines are used to treat anxiety.

Calsequestrin and FKBP inhibit the Ryanodine receptor which is on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. When calcium levels rise, these two molecules are outcompeted and the channel opens, releasing more calcium from the SR.  PKA and cAMP are involved in the phosphorylation of phospholamban which allows calcium to be taken up into the SR more quickly.  Calbindin is involved in the buffering of calcium in the SR.

Spinal stenosis: History is classically ‘neurogenic claudication’ - pain on walking relief on rest. Pain is often bilateral and accompanied by tingling. Extension is often painful and flexion eases the pain. SLR is often negative.  Peripheral arterial disease: Pain is also classically experienced on walking but worse on going uphill. Pathology is unilateral and CRANKY - so often just the calf. Pain is relieved by vasodilation so smoking is a major risk factor. Spinal cord compression: Pain is usually unilateral and worse on walking down hills. Pain is often worse at night and may be accompanied by radicular pain. Extension is often painful and flexion eases the pain. SLR is often positive.  Prolapsed IV disc: Pain is classically worse on walking down hills and worse at night. Pain is often unilateral and accompanied by radicular pain. Extension is often painful and flexion eases the pain. SLR is often positive.  Chronic mechanical back pain: Pain is often bilateral and accompanied by stiffness. Extension is often painful and flexion eases the pain. SLR is often negative.  Metastatic spinal cord compression: Pain is usually worse at night and accompanied by radicular pain. Extension is often painful and flexion eases the pain. SLR is often positive.

Agranulocytosis is a severe form of neutropenia characterised by the near total absence of granulocytes in the blood. Clozapine is known to cause agranulocytosis, which can be triggered by a dose increase or if the drug is started at a high dose. Patients taking Clozapine should be regularly monitored for agranulocytosis by blood tests.
